questions.title: Can You Move the Rake Next to Your Ball?
questions.question: Your golf ball stops next to a bunker. There is a rake lying near your ball and it gets in the way when you try to swing. Can you move the rake before you hit your shot?

choices.text: No. You can't move anything that is close to your ball.
Yes. A rake is something you can move and you can pick it up with no penalty.
Yes, but only if your ball does not move.
No. You must just play around the rake or take a drop.

questions.explanation: You can move a rake if it is in your way, even if it is near your ball. A rake is called a movable obstruction. You will not get a penalty for moving it. If you move the rake and your ball rolls away, just put the ball back where it was. There is still no penalty.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: A sandy area on the golf course that is hard to hit from.
Something that is not part of the course, like a rake or bottle, and you can pick it up or move it.

questions.teachingTip: Show kids how to gently move a rake or other objects near their ball and what to do if their ball moves by accident.
likelyMisconceptions: Kids might think they have to play with the rake in the way.
Kids might worry about getting a penalty for touching or moving a rake.

questions.title: Can You Remove a Rake Before Playing?
questions.question: Your ball comes to rest next to a bunker. A rake is lying on the ground beside your ball and is in the way of your swing. Can you move the rake before playing your shot?

choices.text: No. Once your ball has come to rest, nothing nearby may be moved.
Yes. A rake is a movable obstruction and may be moved without penalty.
Yes, but only if your ball does not move.
No. You must either play around the rake or take unplayable ball relief.

questions.explanation: A bunker rake is a movable obstruction. You may move it at any time without penalty. If moving the rake causes your ball to move, you must replace the ball on its original spot, and there is no penalty for causing it to move while removing a movable obstruction. Many golfers think they have to leave the rake where it is once the ball has come to rest, but that is incorrect. (Rule 15.2a, Rule 15.2a(1))
